title: Compactifiable morphism
statement: Let $f:X\to S$ be a separated finite-type morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-proper-morphism, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. It is *compactifiable* if there exist a scheme $\overline X$, an open immersion $j:X\hookrightarrow\overline X$ [def-weil-open-immersion], and a proper morphism $r:\overline X\to S$ [def-weil-proper-morphism] such that $r\circ j=f$; this factorization is a *compactification* of $f$. In the finite-type-over-a-field setting of this chapter, every separated finite-type morphism $f:X\to S$ between finite-type schemes over a field $k$ is compactifiable. This existence assertion applies to these morphisms, not to the arbitrary base-change morphisms allowed in compact-support base change.

proof.text: For the existence assertion, let $k$ be a field and let $X$ and $S$ be finite-type $k$-schemes, with $f:X\to S$ separated and of finite type. Every ideal of $k$ is either zero or the unit ideal, hence is generated by zero or one element. Thus $k$ is Noetherian by [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. The single affine open $\operatorname{Spec}k$ therefore witnesses that $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is locally Noetherian by [pqf-def-locnoeth]. It is quasi-compact by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-qcqs], so it is Noetherian (locally Noetherian and quasi-compact).

source.place: Tag 01OV, definition-noetherian; the field-ideal argument is elementary

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian] to the finite-type structure morphism $S\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. It gives that $S$ is Noetherian, hence locally Noetherian and quasi-compact. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-locally-noetherian-quasi-separated] to $S$ to obtain that intersections of affine opens are quasi-compact, that is, $S$ is quasi-separated. This supplies both base hypotheses of Nagata's theorem; it does not assume that $S$ is separated over $k$.

Now $f$ is separated and of finite type by hypothesis, and its target $S$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated by the preceding step. The concluding assertion of [thm-nagata-compactification] gives a compactification of $f$, namely an open immersion $j:X\hookrightarrow\overline X$ followed by a proper morphism $r:\overline X\to S$ whose composite is $f$. This is precisely a witness for the definition above. No conclusion about an arbitrary base-change morphism is used.

source.place: Tag 0F41, theorem-nagata; Tag 0ATT, section-compactify (definition of compactification)
